metadata.title: Artificial intelligence in head and neck cancer rehabilitation services: current state and future perspectives
metadata.journal: Current Opinion in Otolaryngology & Head and Neck Surgery

sections.text: Purpose of review This review evaluates the current state of artificial intelligence (AI) in head and neck cancer (HNC) rehabilitation services by mapping current applications across rehabilitation pathways and allied healthcare professionals (AHPs), and outlines future directions and recommendations for integrating AI into routine healthcare. Recent findings HNC care is highly specialized and requires intensive collaboration among many professionals, yet rehabilitation services remain fragmented, and AI developments are limited. More broadly, AI applications are emerging across multiple rehabilitation domains, including speech and swallowing assessment, motion analysis, nutrition support, mental health detection, and administrative automation. The most mature tools with high Technology Readiness Levels (TRLs) support patient education, telehealth communication, and real-time monitoring, particularly in dietetics, physiotherapy, and speech therapy. Low TRLs – such as multidisciplinary decision support, personalized exercise planning, mental health detection, and automated speech disorder assessment – remain in early development. Major barriers include fragmented data infrastructures, limited representativeness of HNC populations, ethical concerns, and the need to preserve the therapeutic patient–provider relationship. large language models (LLMs) show potential for structuring information and generating rehabilitation plans but require expert oversight. Summary AI has the potential to enhance coordinative rehabilitation and shows promise for both health care providers and patients. However, meaningful progress toward clinical implementation requires rigorous validation, the development of shared standards, and strong interdisciplinary collaboration.

Head and neck cancer (HNC) comprises a diverse group of malignancies, affecting the oral cavity, pharynx, larynx, salivary glands, and related structures. HNC ranks as the seventh most common cancer globally, with over 660 000 new diagnoses annually [ 1 ]. Major risk factors include tobacco and alcohol consumption as well as human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, particularly in oropharyngeal cancer [ 2 , 3 ]. Treatment is typically multimodal: combining surgery, radiotherapy, chemoradiotherapy, and, increasingly, immunotherapy [ 4 ]. Despite substantial therapeutic advances, treatment of HNC often results in complex, interrelated impairments affecting body functions such as swallowing, speech, and physical strength, and can have an influence on overall quality of life (QoL) related to social-emotional well being such as anxiety and distress, and physical function [ 5 , 6 ]. These limitations frequently cascade into activity restrictions and participation challenges, as described by the International Classification of Functioning and Disability and Health (ICF). The ICF framework, endorsed by the World Health Organization (WHO), is the international standard to describe and classify health and disability levels [ 7 , 8 ]. For example, dysphagia can lead to malnutrition and muscle wasting, which in turn compromise mobility and social engagement. Psychosocial consequences, such as anxiety or social isolation, may exacerbate functional decline, creating a multidimensional rehabilitation challenge. Evidence supports that structured rehabilitation interventions can improve functional outcomes in HNC patients [ 9 , 10 ]. Ideally, this care is delivered through an interdisciplinary approach, where clinicians and allied health professionals (AHPs) collaborate to address multifactorial problems simultaneously [ 11 ]. However, evidence that such a coordinated interdisciplinary rehabilitation intervention enhances functioning, participation, and quality of life compared to mono-disciplinary rehabilitation interventions is still scarce [ 9 , 12 ]. With the rise of artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare, new opportunities are emerging to optimize healthcare. The foundation of any AI application lies in the quality and diversity of its training data. These data may include imaging data, textual sources for large language models (LLMs), omics datasets, or combinations thereof. Generative AI refers to models that create new content based on learned patterns from input data and represents a rapidly evolving domain within this landscape. The widespread availability of LLMs, accelerated by the introduction of ChatGPT in 2022, has democratized access and enabled researchers and clinicians to experiment with these tools more readily. AI is already widely applied across industries and increasingly in healthcare: supporting surgeons during operations and assisting radiologists. However, a larger group working as AHPs could benefit from these technologies as well [ 13 ▪▪ ]. Therefore, the aim of this paper is to critically examine the role of AI in HNC rehabilitation, both at the level of overall rehabilitation pathways and within the specific AHP disciplines. We will provide an overview of the current landscape of AI applications used in HNC rehabilitation interventions, cancer rehabilitation, or AHP-specific rehabilitation interventions, and discuss future directions and recommendations for integrating AI-driven solutions into routine clinical practice.

sections.section: How Is The Landscape Of Hnc Rehabilitation Organized?
sections.text: Several reviews have assessed the current landscape of HNC rehabilitation and the availability of guidelines for AHPs [ 9 , 12 , 14 , 15 ]. They conclude that HNC rehabilitation is characterized by a fragmented yet progressively expanding continuum of care that spans prehabilitation, treatment-related supportive care, and long-term survivorship management. HNC rehabilitation should preferably be conceptualized using the ICF framework, encompassing not only impairments in body functions and structures, but also activity limitations, and participation restrictions [ 6 , 7 ]. Historically, HNC rehabilitation has focused primarily on impairment-level outcomes, such as swallowing physiology, speech intelligibility, and musculoskeletal dysfunction. By contrast, less attention has been given to activity performance and participation outcomes, including communication, social roles, and return to work [ 10 , 13 ▪▪ ]. In addition, in both research and clinical practice, the term rehabilitation is used inconsistently and sometimes interchangeably with related concepts such as survivorship care, supportive care, or follow-up care. This lack of definitional consensus complicates the development of a common language across AHPs, leading to heterogeneity in care delivery and outcome evaluation [ 16 , 17 ].

sections.section: The Need For Enhanced Interdisciplinary Integration Of Allied Healthcare Professionals
sections.text: Recent reviews demonstrate that rehabilitation interventions addressing multiple ICF domains are delivered by a range of AHPs, such as speech therapy, physical therapy, lymphedema therapy, occupational therapy, nutritional support, and psychosocial care [ 9 , 12 , 15 ]. However, the interventions are often delivered in isolated disciplinary streams and at variable time points across the disease trajectory [ 9 , 15 ]. A recent narrative review about prehabilitation and rehabilitation guidelines for AHPs working in the field of HNC emphasizes structured, evidence-informed prehabilitation and rehabilitation pathways that begin before treatment and extend into survivorship [ 14 ]. Survivorship models increasingly position rehabilitation as a core component of risk-stratified, lifelong care, addressing persistent activity limitations and participation restrictions influenced by personal and environmental factors [ 16 – 18 ]. Overall, despite growing recognition of the effectiveness and potential cost-efficiency of multidimensional rehabilitation, the organization of HNC rehabilitation is provided as multiple single-discipline treatments leading to heterogeneity. This is seen between countries as well as within different centers in one country [ 14 ]. A survey within Dutch HNC centers found significant variation in service organization, professional involvement, and interventions. While speech therapy, physiotherapy, and dietetics are mostly part of the HNC rehabilitation team, occupational therapy, psychology, and social support are less consistently integrated as well as the involvement of the coordinating role of a rehabilitation specialist [ 19 ]. Systematic screening, standardized pathways, and dedicated funding are often lacking, resulting in inequities in patient access to rehabilitation services and outcomes [ 14 , 19 , 20 ]. This is unfortunate, given the existing evidence supporting the effectiveness of interdisciplinary HNC rehabilitation protocols [ 10 , 11 ]. Passchier et al. conducted a feasibility study of a dedicated interdisciplinary HNC rehabilitation program developed at the Netherlands Cancer Institute [ 21 ]. They concluded that 90% of patients achieved their interdisciplinary goals and that patients showed significant improvements in quality of life within seven months [ 11 ]. Similarly, Eades et al. observed improvements in physical function, weight maintenance, symptom reduction, and quality of life after an 8-week rehabilitation program, supporting the added value of a multidisciplinary approach [ 10 ]. AI has the potential to reduce practice variation and promote standardized care pathways; however, its full impact depends on the integration of all AHP disciplines into cohesive rehabilitation strategies. At present, progress toward developing and deploying AI-driven integrated rehabilitation solutions for HNC remains limited. Nevertheless, interest in AI applications among AHPs is increasing, with early studies describing emerging innovations including AI-assisted personalization of rehabilitation plans after head and neck surgery, exploratory use of machine learning (ML)-enabled wearable technologies for monitoring therapeutic exercises, and concept frameworks for adaptive, AI-driven cancer rehabilitation incorporating virtual coaching and remote assessment [ 13 ▪▪ , 22 ▪▪ , 23 ▪▪ ]. Recent research highlights significant advances in the application of ML to the evaluation and management of speech, voice, and swallowing in HNC patients [ 24 ]. While these developments signal important progress, most remain at the proof-of-concept stage, emphasizing the need for large-scale, multiinstitutional validation and integration into clinical practice [ 24 ].

sections.section: Progress Within Individual Allied Healthcare Professional Disciplines Supporting Rehabilitation Care
sections.text: After an extensive literature search, an overview of current AI applications and their technology readiness for use in rehabilitation services more broadly is provided in Table 1 . The applications are divided into general healthcare tools and AHP-specific applications for prevention and diagnosis [ 28 – 35 ▪ ], therapy and planning [ 13 , 23 ▪▪ , 27 , 28 , 31 , 35 – 37 ▪ , 38 , 39 ▪ , 40 ], follow-up and monitoring [ 31 ▪ , 37 ▪ , 41 ▪ ] and administration and education [ 13 ▪▪ , 25 , 26 ▪ , 27 ▪ ]. These innovations collectively illustrate AI's expanding role in making rehabilitation more accessible, personalized, and effective. Technology readiness levels (TRLs) were assessed using the TRL framework originally developed by NASA and adapted for health-care innovation by BRIDGE2HE [ 42 ], with a graphical overview shown in Fig. 1 . The studies summarized in Table 1 demonstrate that AI is increasingly being applied within rehabilitation and allied health domains, with considerable variation in TRLs. The most mature developments – those with higher TRLs – are found in prevention & diagnosis, and therapy, particularly within physical therapy, dietetics, and speech therapy. These applications contain tools for monitoring food intake, movement, and activity patterns, and voice and speech parameters, often supported by wearable devices [ 13 ▪▪ , 25 , 26 – 28 , 31 , 32 ▪ , 38 ]. Such integration enables real-time data collection and transfer into clinical applications, facilitating personalized rehabilitation plans and continuous monitoring of patient progress. The majority of AI tools currently available serve supportive roles in education and clinical decision-making, with the reduction of administrative tasks emerging as a quick and impactful benefit. The table also highlights specific high-impact applications, such as AI-assisted videofluoroscopic swallowing study (VFSS) analysis, which can significantly reduce the time burden on speech therapists while improving consistency and reliability [ 30 ▪ ]. In contrast, the lowest TRL applications were identified in multidisciplinary domains, such as AI-assisted clinical decision-making for risk prediction. Similarly low TRLs were observed in AHP-specific applications, including AI-supported personalized diagnosis and exercise planning in physiotherapy, early mental health detection in psychotherapy, and automated voice disorder assessment in speech therapy [ 23 ▪▪ , 29 , 33 – 37 , 39 ▪ , 40 , 41 ▪ ]. These lower TRLs applications require further development and validation for clinical integration.

sections.section: The Use Of Large Language Models In Rehabilitation Planning
sections.text: LLMs offer potential for structuring fragmented information and generating evidence-based recommendations to support clinical reasoning. Marcaccini et al. exemplify this approach by generating rehabilitation programs for patients undergoing head and neck surgery using four different language models [ 23 ▪▪ ]. Their study employed fictional cases and carefully designed prompts to compare outputs. Results showed that LLMs can generate HNC rehabilitation programs with varying quality and readability. ChatGPT-4o produced the most clinically relevant plans, while Gemini 2 generated more readable content. However, it is critical to recognize that LLMs are statistical models without an intrinsic understanding of content. Therefore, having a knowledgeable expert involved in the development and critical assessment of the output is key to create use-able content. An iterative workflow combining expert input and curated sources may further enhance output quality. For instance, when generating fictional cases for HNC rehabilitation programs, prompts should specify case characteristics (e.g., tumor origin, treatment modalities, TNM staging). Subsequent iterations can incorporate local clinical guidelines (e.g., NCCN guidelines [ 40 ], treatment guidelines [ 41 ▪ ]), and frameworks such as those proposed by Tschiesner et al. [ 7 , 8 ] alongside clinic-specific details, including AHPs roles, to support interdisciplinary collaboration around shared rehabilitation goals and to refine goal setting and treatment plans. Despite these advances, clinical adoption of AI tools remains limited. As of 2025, only two FDA-approved AI tools exist for HNC applications for radiology purposes (i.e. RapidAI Lumina 3D and GE HealthCare MR Contour DL) , and none for rehabilitation [ 43 ]. The slow adoption of evidence-based digital technologies in routine cancer care clinics has been observed before [ 44 ]. The following section will address key challenges regarding use of AI in rehabilitation to support progress in the field.

sections.section: Critical Reflection Regarding Use Of Ai In Rehabilitation
sections.text: While AI holds great promise for healthcare, its integration into rehabilitation brings both practical and ethical challenges. Beyond the general principles of responsible AI, such as explainability, transparency, and mitigation of bias, there are several rehabilitation-specific considerations [ 27 ▪ , 45 ].

sections.section: Interdisciplinary Collaboration For Responsible Ai Integration
sections.text: As shown in Table 1 , many AI applications in HNC rehabilitation are still in early developmental phases and discipline specific. This underscores the need for stronger collaboration and more integrated efforts to embed AI into rehabilitation practices. Hulsen and Scheper stress that AHPs must be actively involved in AI development, given the novelty of these tools and the importance of addressing ethical considerations, community acceptance, and practical implementation strategies [ 13 ▪▪ ]. Similarly, Hao et al. emphasize transparency and co-creation as critical principles to ensure that solutions are both clinically relevant and aligned with patient needs [ 22 ▪▪ ]. These multiple professional perspectives are crucial to solve inconsistent data inputs, incomplete patient trajectories, and difficulty learning from real-world practice to achieve a holistic approach that ultimately benefits patients.

sections.section: Bias And Representativeness In The Head And Neck Cancer Population
sections.text: A primary concern is the quality and availability of input data for AI systems. Ideally, data should be consolidated within interoperable infrastructures, yet in practice, data sources remain highly fragmented. This fragmentation increases the risk of mispredicting functional outcomes, limits generalizability across patient subgroups, and may inadvertently reinforce existing inequities. These challenges are particularly pronounced in HNC, a rare disease in which AI training datasets, much like clinical trial populations, often fail to capture the full diversity of patient characteristics [ 27 ▪ ].

sections.section: The Patient–Provider Relationship Is Central In Head And Neck Cancer Rehabilitation
sections.text: The patient–provider relationship is central in HNC rehabilitation, and evidence consistently shows that its quality strongly influences clinical outcomes [ 46 , 47 ]. As AI tools enter rehabilitation practice, patient-centered design is essential to ensure that technology enhances, rather than replaces, this therapeutic connection. While psychosocial support delivered through chatbots can provide scalable, on-demand, and cost-effective assistance, human interaction in rehabilitation remains paramount [ 33 ▪ ]. Successful implementation also depends on acceptance by both patients and healthcare professionals. Ethical considerations including privacy, algorithmic bias, and patient autonomy, must be addressed, and AHPs require targeted training to develop the digital competencies needed for effective integration. Ultimately, AI should be viewed as a supportive tool that complements, rather than substitutes, human expertise, as the therapeutic relationship remains fundamental to patient care.

sections.section: Future Perspectives And Recommendations For Ai In Head And Neck Cancer Rehabilitation Services
sections.text: To successfully enable the potential of AI in HNC rehabilitation, the following steps are needed. A clear and shared definition of rehabilitation is essential to enable the effective integration of AI into HNC rehabilitation. Research and testing are essential to validate the efficacy and safety of AI tools within clinical rehabilitation contexts. Integration efforts should align AI solutions with existing care pathways and electronic health record systems. The development of policy frameworks, encompassing (local) guidelines, funding mechanisms, and ethical standards, are needed for responsible adoption. Finally, collaboration between technological and healthcare disciplines is necessary for continuous monitoring and optimization of AI tools into HNC rehabilitation.

HNC rehabilitation is widely acknowledged as essential to patient care, but heterogeneity in terminology, guidelines, variation in service provision, and persistent implementation barriers limit its effectiveness [ 12 , 17 ]. Harmonization of protocols, expansion of evidence-based interventions, and detailed guidance for AHPs across functional disciplines are urgently needed. AI can advance collaboration and reduce variation in clinical practice. AI applications in rehabilitation show the highest TRL in patient education, counseling, telehealth communication, and real-time monitoring for dietetics, physiotherapy, and speech therapy, while lower readiness technologies focus on multidisciplinary decision support, personalized exercise plans, mental health detection, and automated speech disorder assessment. In multidisciplinary collaborations, the assistance of LLMs is well evaluated in fictional cases, but the future lies in reducing labor-intensive work and integrating assistive technologies between multiple AHPs in real-world clinical settings [ 23 ▪▪ ]. We therefore recommend investing in multidisciplinary collaboration to accelerate AI development and implementation, ultimately improving the full trajectory of HNC care: from diagnosis to treatment and rehabilitation.
